claim: Listeria monocytogenes hijacks host actin to promote its intracellular motility and intercellular spread.
source: Listeria monocytogenes hijacks host actin to promote its intracellular motility and intercellular spread.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread proceeds anisotropically in an epithelial monolayer in culture.
source: Here, we use live microscopy and statistical modeling to demonstrate that L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread proceeds anisotropically in an epithelial monolayer in culture.
evidence: The claim is supported by live microscopy data and statistical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Boundaries of infection foci are irregular and dominated by rare pioneer bacteria that spread farther than the rest.
source: We show that boundaries of infection foci are irregular and dominated by rare pioneer bacteria that spread farther than the rest.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy observations and quantitative analysis of infection foci shapes.

claim: Heterogeneous spreading behavior can improve the chances of creating a persistent L. monocytogenes infection in an actively extruding epithelium.
source: We extend our quantitative model for bacterial spread to show that heterogeneous spreading behavior can improve the chances of creating a persistent L. monocytogenes infection in an actively extruding epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by computational simulations that model bacterial spread in the context of host cell extrusion.

claim: L. monocytogenes can spread directly from the cytoplasm of an infected host cell into the cytoplasm of another host cell without exposure to the extracellular milieu.
source: This ubiquitous Gram-positive bacterium can invade and replicate within non-phagocytic cells and, importantly, use a form of actin-based motility to spread directly from the cytoplasm of an infected host cell into the cytoplasm of another host cell without exposure to the extracellular milieu (Tilney and Portnoy, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by Tilney and Portnoy, 1989.

claim: Cell-to-cell spread enables L. monocytogenes to breach and colonize the intestinal epithelium and to subsequently reach distant organs including the liver and brain in immunocompromised patients and the placenta in pregnant women.
source: This process, known as cell-to-cell spread, enables L. monocytogenes to breach and colonize the intestinal epithelium and to subsequently reach distant organs including the liver and brain in immunocompromised patients (Ghosh et al., 2018) and the placenta in pregnant women (Faralla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2018 and Faralla et al., 2016.

claim: Mutant L. monocytogenes strains incapable of undergoing cell-to-cell spread are three orders of magnitude less virulent in murine models compared to wild-type L. monocytogenes.
source: Indeed, compared to wild-type L. monocytogenes, mutant strains incapable of undergoing cell-to-cell spread are three orders of magnitude less virulent in murine models (Domann et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Domann et al., 1992.

claim: L. monocytogenes preferentially adheres to and invades an epithelium at the tips of intestinal villi.
source: L. monocytogenes preferentially adheres to and invades an epithelium at the tips of intestinal villi (Pentecost et al., 2006), where epithelial cells are actively extruded and shed (Sancho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pentecost et al., 2006 and Sancho et al., 2004.

claim: L. monocytogenes uses the protein ActA to polymerize actin at its surface and create an actin comet tail.
source: To initiate cell-to-cell spread, L. monocytogenes uses the protein ActA to polymerize actin at its surface and create an actin comet tail (Pistor et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pistor et al., 1994.

claim: Actin polymerization generates a propulsive force that allows the bacterium to move within the host cytoplasm.
source: Actin polymerization generates a propulsive force that allows the bacterium to move within the host cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin-based bacterial motility.

claim: L. monocytogenes can create protrusions more than ten microns long.
source: Although cell-to-cell spread has been primarily studied as a mechanism of bacterial dissemination between adjacent host cells, it is well established that L. monocytogenes can create protrusions more than ten microns long (Pust et al., 2005), which could, in principle, mediate bacterial spread between two non-adjacent host cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pust et al., 2005.

claim: The bacterial protein internalin C helps L. monocytogenes to relax cortical tension and increase the rate of bacterial-mediated protrusion formation to promote spread.
source: The bacterial protein internalin C helps L. monocytogenes to relax cortical tension and increase the rate of bacterial-mediated protrusion formation to promote spread (Rajabian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rajabian et al., 2009.

claim: TIM4 allows the host to sense bacterial-mediated membrane damage, which then triggers a repair mechanism that L. monocytogenes exploits to promote spread.
source: From the perspective of the host cell, it has been shown that TIM4 allows the host to sense bacterial-mediated membrane damage, which then triggers a repair mechanism that L. monocytogenes exploits to promote spread (Czuczman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Czuczman et al., 2014.

claim: The diaphanous-related formins have been shown to localize to bacteria-containing protrusions and inhibition of their activity decreases the efficiency of cell-to-cell spread.
source: The diaphanous-related formins (Fattouh et al., 2015) and members of the ERM protein family (Pust et al., 2005) have been shown to localize to bacteria-containing protrusions and inhibition of their activity decreases the efficiency of cell-to-cell spread.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fattouh et al., 2015 and Pust et al., 2005.

claim: Members of the ERM protein family have been shown to localize to bacteria-containing protrusions and inhibition of their activity decreases the efficiency of cell-to-cell spread.
source: The diaphanous-related formins (Fattouh et al., 2015) and members of the ERM protein family (Pust et al., 2005) have been shown to localize to bacteria-containing protrusions and inhibition of their activity decreases the efficiency of cell-to-cell spread.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fattouh et al., 2015 and Pust et al., 2005.

claim: MDCK epithelial cells form polarized and homogeneous monolayers in culture.
source: As a model host cell, we chose Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) epithelial cells because they form polarized and homogeneous monolayers in culture (Mays et al., 1995) and have been widely used to study L. monocytogenes infection (Robbins et al., 1999; Pentecost et al., 2006; Pentecost et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mays et al., 1995, Robbins et al., 1999, Pentecost et al., 2006, and Pentecost et al., 2010.

claim: MDCK cells have been widely used to study L. monocytogenes infection.
source: As a model host cell, we chose Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) epithelial cells because they form polarized and homogeneous monolayers in culture (Mays et al., 1995) and have been widely used to study L. monocytogenes infection (Robbins et al., 1999; Pentecost et al., 2006; Pentecost et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robbins et al., 1999, Pentecost et al., 2006, and Pentecost et al., 2010.

claim: The actA promoter becomes transcriptionally active when the bacterium enters the host cell cytosol.
source: We infected confluent MDCK monolayers with a wild-type 10403 S L. monocytogenes strain that contains an mTagRFP open reading frame under the actA promoter, which becomes transcriptionally active when the bacterium enters the host cell cytosol (Moors et al., 1999; Zeldovich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moors et al., 1999 and Zeldovich et al., 2011.

claim: Gentamicin is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that cannot cross the host cell plasma membrane.
source: The presence of gentamicin, a bacteriostatic antibiotic that cannot cross the host cell plasma membrane (Portnoy et al., 1988), during live imaging ensured that only intracellular bacteria contributed to the growth and spread of the infection focus.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Portnoy et al., 1988.

claim: The edges of the boundary of the infection focus were dominated by a small number of bacteria that spread farther than the rest.
source: Given that bacterial invasion of a polarized MDCK monolayer is a rare event (Pentecost et al., 2006), each infection focus most likely began with a single bacterium entering a host cell's cytosol. Due to the clonal nature of the replicating bacteria, and the homogeneity of the host monolayer, we were surprised to find behavioral heterogeneity within the bacterial population; the edges of the boundary of the infection focus, determined by the smallest boundary that completely encloses all bacteria, were dominated by a small number of bacteria that spread farther than the rest (Figure 1A, white arrows in third panel).
evidence: This is supported by direct observation in microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Far-spreading bacteria, referred to as 'pioneers', nearly always created irregular boundaries by the end of the experiment.
source: Although each focus may have started out roughly circular, far-spreading bacteria, which we refer to as 'pioneers', nearly always created irregular boundaries by the end of the experiment (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Intracellular bacterial replication was approximately exponential.
source: Despite boundary irregularity, intracellular bacterial replication was approximately exponential (Figure 1C), and the growth rate could be modeled with a one-term exponential function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with an average doubling time of approximately 180 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of bacterial fluorescence intensity over time shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The average doubling time of intracellular L. monocytogenes is approximately 180 min.
source: Despite boundary irregularity, intracellular bacterial replication was approximately exponential (Figure 1C), and the growth rate could be modeled with a one-term exponential function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) with an average doubling time of approximately 180 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is calculated from exponential fits to experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The doubling time of approximately 180 min is comparable to what has been previously reported in other epithelial host cell types using gentamicin protection assays.
source: This doubling time is comparable to what has been previously reported in other epithelial host cell types using gentamicin protection assays (Gaillard et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gaillard et al., 1987.

claim: Between 360 and 960 min post-infection, the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the bacterial positions appeared linear.
source: Between 360 and 960 min post-infection, the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the bacterial positions (defined here as the second moment of the fluorescence intensity distribution) appeared linear (Figure 1C), which is consistent with a random walk (Berg, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with random walk theory cited from Berg, 1993.

claim: Linear MSD is consistent with a random walk.
source: Between 360 and 960 min post-infection, the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the bacterial positions (defined here as the second moment of the fluorescence intensity distribution) appeared linear (Figure 1C), which is consistent with a random walk (Berg, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berg, 1993.

claim: The slope of the MSD increased with time.
source: However, the slope of the MSD was not always constant, but instead increased with time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with the appearance of fast-spreading organisms within a migrating population (Shigesada et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and is consistent with theory cited from Shigesada et al., 1995.

claim: An increasing MSD slope is consistent with the appearance of fast-spreading organisms within a migrating population.
source: However, the slope of the MSD was not always constant, but instead increased with time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with the appearance of fast-spreading organisms within a migrating population (Shigesada et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shigesada et al., 1995.

claim: There is no correlation between bacterial growth rate and MSD.
source: We found no correlation between bacterial growth rate and MSD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), enabling us to treat these two parameters as independent in the quantitative model described below.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Random movement and growth starting from a point source should yield isotropic shapes.
source: From the literature, it is expected that, when starting from a point source, random movement and growth should yield isotropic shapes (Holmes et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Holmes et al., 1994.

claim: The reaction-diffusion equation yields circular infection foci that grow in size and intensity over time.
source: Because Equation 1 is radially isotropic, its solutions correspond to circular infection foci that grow in size and intensity over time (Figure 2A and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by solving the reaction-diffusion equation and visualizing the results in Figure 2A and Video 2.

claim: A continuum model cannot account for the experimentally observed heterogeneous focus shapes.
source: Such a continuum model cannot account for the experimentally observed heterogeneous focus shapes.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between the isotropic solutions of the continuum model and the anisotropic experimental observations.

claim: Stochastic simulations generated foci that were approximately circular and thus differed significantly from the experimental foci.
source: While not perfectly isotropic, the stochastic simulations generated foci that were approximately circular and thus differed significantly from the experimental foci (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulated and experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Simulated foci are substantially more circular than experimental foci.
source: The data showed that simulated foci are substantially more circular than experimental foci (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative circularity measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Intracellular L. monocytogenes motility exhibits directional persistence over time-scales of a few minutes.
source: It is known that intracellular L. monocytogenes does not undergo truly uncorrelated random walks as was assumed in our simulations. Instead, intracellular L. monocytogenes motility, aided by ActA-dependent actin comet tails, exhibits directional persistence over time-scales of a few minutes (Lacayo and Theriot, 2004; Soo and Theriot, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lacayo and Theriot, 2004 and Soo and Theriot, 2005.

claim: L. monocytogenes can ricochet off MDCK host cell boundaries at a frequency dependent on monolayer age.
source: In fact, it has been shown that L. monocytogenes can ricochet off MDCK host cell boundaries at a frequency dependent on monolayer age (Robbins et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Robbins et al., 1999.

claim: Bacterial motility persistence and the presence of host cell boundaries do not significantly affect the circularity of simulated foci.
source: We found that neither of these two conditions affects circularity significantly; specifically, foci simulated with these features are only about 3% less circular than foci simulated by a random walk alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Changing the probability with which the bacteria cross host cell boundaries had a minimal effect on the circularity of the simulated foci.
source: Overall, changing the probability with which the bacteria cross host cell boundaries had a minimal effect on the circularity of the simulated foci (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread cannot be modeled with only a random walk and exponential growth.
source: Taken together, our experimental and simulated data show that L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread cannot be modeled with only a random walk and exponential growth, and that the presence of host cell boundaries and the persistence of bacterial motility do not have a significant effect on the circularity of infection foci.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of experimental and simulated data showing that simple random walk models do not reproduce experimental observations.

claim: For experiments performed in the presence of extracellular gentamicin, L. monocytogenes only replicates in a host cell's cytoplasm.
source: For our experiments performed in the presence of extracellular gentamicin, L. monocytogenes only replicates in a host cell's cytoplasm.
evidence: This is based on the known property that gentamicin cannot cross the host cell plasma membrane, as cited earlier.

claim: At least one round of division must take place before bacteria can resume actin-based motility in the recipient cell.
source: We also know from direct observation that at least one round of division must take place before bacteria can resume actin-based motility in the recipient cell (Robbins et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Robbins et al., 1999.

claim: Pioneer bacteria can reach a non-adjacent recipient host cell in less than 30 min.
source: Importantly, this bacterium can reach a non-adjacent recipient host cell in less than 30 min even though it takes an MDCK cell approximately 45 min to complete the process of taking up a bacterium-containing protrusion (Robbins et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microscopy data and comparison with the known uptake time cited from Robbins et al., 1999.

claim: It takes an MDCK cell approximately 45 min to complete the process of taking up a bacterium-containing protrusion.
source: Importantly, this bacterium can reach a non-adjacent recipient host cell in less than 30 min even though it takes an MDCK cell approximately 45 min to complete the process of taking up a bacterium-containing protrusion (Robbins et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Robbins et al., 1999.

claim: Non-pioneer bacteria typically move about 1–2 µm in 5-min intervals in the assay.
source: In contrast, non-pioneer bacteria typically move about 1–2 µm in 5-min intervals in our assay (Video 6).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from microscopy data shown in Video 6.

claim: The presence of pioneers caused the simulated boundaries to become anisotropic, particularly in the early steps of the simulation.
source: As expected, the presence of pioneers caused the simulated boundaries to become anisotropic, particularly in the early steps of the simulation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Simulations with pioneers recapitulated the increase in the MSD slope during the later time points of the experimental data.
source: Additionally, these simulations recapitulated the increase in the MSD slope during the later time points of the experimental data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A probability of 0.10 allowed, on average, approximately 75% of bacteria to have a pioneer ancestor or be pioneers themselves by the end of the simulation.
source: A probability of 0.10 allowed, on average, approximately 75% of bacteria to have a pioneer ancestor or be pioneers themselves by the end of the simulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Simulated foci boundaries tended to be more anisotropic during earlier steps of the simulation, and they became more circular as simulation time increased.
source: It is likely that the approach towards a pioneer majority explains why simulated foci boundaries tended to be more anisotropic during earlier steps of the simulation, and why they became more circular as simulation time increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Experimental circularity is equivalent to the circularity seen for simulations with pioneer probabilities of 10−3 and 10−2.
source: We confirmed these findings quantitatively and showed that experimental circularity is equivalent to the circularity seen for simulations with pioneer probabilities of 10−3 and 10−2 (Figure 3D), which suggests that during our cell-to-cell spread experimental assay, approximately 1.4% to 12% of bacteria have pioneer ancestors or are pioneers themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of experimental and simulated circularity data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: During the cell-to-cell spread experimental assay, approximately 1.4% to 12% of bacteria have pioneer ancestors or are pioneers themselves.
source: We confirmed these findings quantitatively and showed that experimental circularity is equivalent to the circularity seen for simulations with pioneer probabilities of 10−3 and 10−2 (Figure 3D), which suggests that during our cell-to-cell spread experimental assay, approximately 1.4% to 12% of bacteria have pioneer ancestors or are pioneers themselves (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of experimental and simulated circularity data and the calculation of pioneer fractions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A larger Dfast/Dslow ratio decreases circularity significantly more than a smaller ratio.
source: As expected, a larger ratio, that is pioneers taking longer steps than non-pioneers, decreases circularity significantly more than a smaller ratio (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread is consistent with individual bacteria having a low but non-zero probability of becoming pioneers, while the majority of the bacteria spread locally.
source: Together our findings suggest that L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread is consistent with individual bacteria having a low but non-zero probability of becoming pioneers, while the majority of the bacteria spread locally.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental and simulation results showing that a small fraction of pioneers can explain the observed anisotropic spread patterns.

claim: L. monocytogenes' ability to create long, pioneer-containing protrusions is critical for the complex, non-circular boundaries observed in experimental data.
source: L. monocytogenes' ability to create long, pioneer-containing protrusions thus would be critical for the complex, non-circular boundaries observed in experimental data.
evidence: This is inferred from the hypothesis that pioneers spread via long protrusions and the observation that pioneers determine the irregular boundaries.

claim: The GRR mutant is less persistent than wild-type bacteria, which means that it loses its original direction more quickly than wild-type bacteria.
source: This mutant, known as the glycine-rich repeat (GRR) mutant, is less persistent than wild-type bacteria, which means that it loses its original direction more quickly than wild-type bacteria.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of the GRR mutant from prior research.

claim: The GRR mutant is characterized by two-fold shorter actin comet tails.
source: The GRR mutant is also characterized by two-fold shorter actin comet tails (Auerbuch et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Auerbuch et al., 2003.

claim: GRR mutant foci were significantly more circular than foci created by wild-type L. monocytogenes.
source: Upon quantifying the circularity of GRR foci, we found that they were significantly more circular than foci created by wild-type L. monocytogenes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative circularity measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The increased circularity of GRR foci was likely a consequence of a decrease in the probability of forming long, straight protrusions.
source: This was likely a consequence of a decrease in the probability of forming long, straight protrusions, which then decreased the probability of bacteria exhibiting pioneer behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of the GRR mutant and the observed increase in circularity.

claim: Changing the directional persistence in simulations including pioneers had little effect on circularity.
source: Indeed, changing the directional persistence in simulations including pioneers had little effect in circularity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), thus supporting the idea that pioneer behavior, that is making long straight protrusions, has a stronger effect in circularity than intracellular directional persistence.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pioneer behavior has a stronger effect on circularity than intracellular directional persistence.
source: Indeed, changing the directional persistence in simulations including pioneers had little effect in circularity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), thus supporting the idea that pioneer behavior, that is making long straight protrusions, has a stronger effect in circularity than intracellular directional persistence.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of simulation results with different parameters.

claim: L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread is heterogeneous as it proceeds via local non-pioneers and far-spreading pioneers, each of which can be modeled with a random walk.
source: Our findings suggest that L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread is heterogeneous as it proceeds via local non-pioneers and far-spreading pioneers, each of which can be modeled with a random walk.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental and simulation results.

claim: Pioneer behavior is probably based on L. monocytogenes' ability to spread directly to non-adjacent host cells via long extracellular protrusions.
source: In addition, we have shown that pioneer behavior is probably based on L. monocytogenes' ability to spread directly to non-adjacent host cells via long extracellular protrusions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of pioneer bacteria and the properties of long protrusions.

claim: Values of Dfast that were 60- to 90-fold higher than Dslow allowed L. monocytogenes to reach a stable steady state in simulations with host cell extrusion.
source: Interestingly, values of Dfast that were 60- to 90-fold higher than Dslow allowed L. monocytogenes to reach a stable steady state (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A Dfast/Dslow ratio of 60- to 90-fold translates to pioneer bacteria taking steps 7.4- to 9.5-fold longer as compared to non-pioneer bacteria.
source: A Dfast/Dslow ratio in this range translates to pioneer bacteria taking steps 7.4- to 9.5-fold longer as compared to non-pioneer bacteria, which is consistent with our experimental observations (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is calculated from the diffusion coefficient ratio and is consistent with experimental observations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: L. monocytogenes heterogeneous cell-to-cell spread improves the chances of the pathogen reaching a stable steady state in vivo as compared to bacteria spreading via a random walk alone.
source: Together, our findings argue that L. monocytogenes heterogeneous cell-to-cell spread improves the chances of the pathogen reaching a stable steady state in vivo as compared to bacteria spreading via a random walk alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing that heterogeneous spread increases the probability of stable steady state outcomes.

claim: Stable steady state would prevent damage to the host animal tissue, facilitate bacterial dissemination to other host animals, and allow L. monocytogenes to thrive in the actively extruding and ever-changing intestinal epithelium.
source: The combination of these outcomes would prevent damage to the host animal tissue, facilitate bacterial dissemination to other host animals, and allow L. monocytogenes to thrive in the actively extruding and ever-changing intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the definition and implications of stable steady state in the context of host-pathogen interactions.

claim: Plaque assays have been used to study late stages of L. monocytogenes infection where a few millions of bacteria have created plaques—sites of host cell death in cultured epithelial monolayers.
source: First, plaque assays have been used to study late stages of infection where a few millions of bacteria have created plaques—sites of host cell death in cultured epithelial monolayers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plaque assays in the field.

claim: The size of the plaque correlates to the efficiency of spread.
source: The size of the plaque correlates to the efficiency of spread (Van Langendonck et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Van Langendonck et al., 1998.

claim: Late stages of L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread create circular plaques.
source: We developed this null hypothesis because (1) there is no evidence in the literature to suggest that intracellular L. monocytogenes motility has directionality, (2) late stages of L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread create circular plaques (Van Langendonck et al., 1998), and (3) MDCK cells form compact and relatively homogeneous monolayers in culture (Mays et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Van Langendonck et al., 1998.

claim: Allowing each bacterium to choose between two behaviors, far-reaching pioneer and local non-pioneer, approximated the shape of the experimental data better than simulating a single behavior of spreading bacteria.
source: Through simulations, we have found that allowing each bacterium to choose between two behaviors, far-reaching pioneer and local non-pioneer, approximated the shape of the experimental data better than simulating a single behavior of spreading bacteria (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Simulated foci became less circular when the ratio Dfast/Dslow was high and the total number of pioneer bacteria in the infection focus was very small (yet non-zero).
source: Simulated foci became less circular when the ratio Dfast/Dslow was high and the total number of pioneer bacteria in the infection focus was very small (yet non-zero).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing the relationship between pioneer parameters and circularity.

claim: Small absolute numbers of pioneers are required in order to generate non-circular foci shapes as a result of stochastic fluctuations.
source: Because pioneer bacteria themselves are assumed to not have a preferred spreading direction, small absolute numbers of pioneers are required in order to generate non-circular foci shapes as a result of stochastic fluctuations.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results and the stochastic nature of the model.

claim: Properties of the bacteria themselves contribute significantly to infection focus anisotropy.
source: While we cannot rule out the possibility that infection focus anisotropy can also be attributed in part to host cell heterogeneity, the L. monocytogenes GRR mutant data suggest that properties of the bacteria themselves contribute significantly to this phenomenon.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRR mutant experimental results showing increased circularity.

claim: The GRR mutant L. monocytogenes creates shorter extracellular protrusions than wild-type bacteria.
source: Given that changing directional persistence in our simulations had little to no effect on circularity, but that changing Dfast/Dslow did, it is likely that the GRR mutant L. monocytogenes creates shorter extracellular protrusions, that is GRR pioneers take shorter steps than wild-type pioneers.
evidence: This is inferred from the GRR mutant experimental results and simulation results.

claim: In the intestinal epithelium, which is characterized by a dense and highly organized apical brush border, it is probably more likely that pioneers would spread either laterally between cells in the epithelium or basally at the junction between the enterocytes and the subjacent basement membrane.
source: Whereas at least a few of the pioneer events that we directly observed in MDCK cells appear to involve long apical protrusions, in the intestinal epithelium, which is characterized by a dense and highly organized apical brush border (Crawley et al., 2014), it is probably more likely that pioneers would spread either laterally between cells in the epithelium or basally at the junction between the enterocytes and the subjacent basement membrane.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known structure of the intestinal epithelium cited from Crawley et al., 2014.

claim: L. monocytogenes' ability to cross the basal membrane of an epithelium via an actin-dependent process has been well-characterized.
source: Indeed, L. monocytogenes' ability to cross the basal membrane of an epithelium via an actin-dependent process has been well-characterized (Faralla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Faralla et al., 2018.

claim: Intracellular pathogens that spread from cell to cell without making extracellular protrusions would be expected to spread via a process resembling a random walk.
source: An extension of our model then argues that intracellular pathogens that spread from cell to cell without making extracellular protrusions would be expected to spread via a process resembling a random walk.
evidence: This is inferred from the model that pioneers spread via long protrusions.

claim: Burkholderia thailandensis spreads intercellularly primarily by inducing the cytoplasmic fusion of two neighboring host cells.
source: The Gram-negative bacillus Burkholderia thailandensis is an example of a bacterial pathogen that spreads intercellularly primarily by inducing the cytoplasmic fusion of two neighboring host cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B. thailandensis.

claim: Infection foci created by B. thailandensis in mammalian host cells are significantly more isotropic than those created by wild-type L. monocytogenes.
source: Indeed, consistent with our pioneer model, infection foci created by B. thailandensis in mammalian host cells are significantly more isotropic than those created by wild-type L. monocytogenes (French et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to French et al., 2011.

claim: The rice-water weevil, Lissorhoptrus orzyzophilus, migrates by both crawling and flying.
source: For example, the rice-water weevil, Lissorhoptrus orzyzophilus, migrates by both crawling and flying (Shigesada et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shigesada et al., 1995.

claim: The mean squared displacement accelerates with time in both rice-water weevil migration pattern data and L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread live microscopy assays.
source: This ecological model parallels our heterogeneous L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread model given that: (1) the mean squared displacement accelerates with time in both rice-water weevil migration pattern data and L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread live microscopy assays (Shigesada et al., 1995), (2) the migration boundary of this organism deviates from a circle similar to bacterial infection foci (Andow et al., 1990), and (3) the rice-water weevil bimodal migration mechanism resembles that of bacterial local spread versus pioneer spread in long protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shigesada et al., 1995.

claim: The migration boundary of the rice-water weevil deviates from a circle similar to bacterial infection foci.
source: This ecological model parallels our heterogeneous L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread model given that: (1) the mean squared displacement accelerates with time in both rice-water weevil migration pattern data and L. monocytogenes cell-to-cell spread live microscopy assays (Shigesada et al., 1995), (2) the migration boundary of this organism deviates from a circle similar to bacterial infection foci (Andow et al., 1990), and (3) the rice-water weevil bimodal migration mechanism resembles that of bacterial local spread versus pioneer spread in long protrusions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andow et al., 1990.

claim: Vaccinia virus can accelerate its own rate of spread by inducing the expression of viral proteins on the surface of an infected host cell that repel superinfecting virions.
source: In addition, vaccinia virus can accelerate its own rate of spread by inducing the expression of viral proteins on the surface of an infected host cell. Upon encountering those proteins, new incoming viral particles are repelled from the already-infected host cells by actin projections and encouraged to infect virus-free host cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vaccinia virus superinfection exclusion.

source: For example, a well-characterized mathematical model is the Lévy flight, a random walk model where the step sizes are drawn from a heavy-tailed distribution instead of a normal distribution, thus ensuring a non-trivial fraction of arbitrary long steps (Dubkov et al., 2008).

source: Given that it is a foodborne pathogen, L. monocytogenes infections begin in the host's alimentary canal. In this work, we propose that L. monocytogenes may have evolved the ability to spread via host cell skipping to maximize its chances of surviving, replicating, and spreading in a host's actively extruding intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is speculated based on the simulation results showing that heterogeneous spread improves survival in extruding epithelia.
